again/loop: A language model writes one token at a time. Run it on the text so far, pick a next token from the last position, add it to the end, and run it again.
again/redo: Each run starts from scratch. Attention in every block needs a key and a value for every token, so each run computes them all again, though only the last token is new.
again/same: And the old ones come out the same every time. The causal mask lets a token read only itself and the tokens before it, so a token added at the end changes nothing earlier, in any block.
again/count: Count the keys one block computes. Step one computes one key, step two computes two, and step ten computes ten.
again/area: Together they fill a staircase. Turn a copy upside down and fit it on top, and the two make a rectangle, ten by eleven. One staircase is half of it: fifty-five keys.
again/formula: That works for any number of steps, T. The rectangle is T by T plus one, and the staircase is half of it: T times T plus one, over two.
again/thousand: So writing a thousand tokens computes five hundred thousand five hundred keys in each block: about half a million.
cache/keep: So compute each key and value once, and keep it. That store is the KV cache: K for keys, and V for values. Every block keeps one.
cache/name: Cache was French Canadian trappers' word for a hidden store of supplies. In 1968, J S Liptay described the cache of an I B M computer: a small, fast memory that keeps data close at hand, to use again.
cache/step: Now each step computes a query, a key and a value for the newest token only. Its key and value join the cache, and its query attends over everything stored there.
cache/slide: Each row is the row above, carried down unchanged, plus one new token.
cache/q: Queries are not kept. A query is used once, by its own token, at its own step. Later tokens need only the earlier keys, to score against, and values, to blend.
cache/work: So ten steps compute ten keys instead of fifty-five, one per token. A thousand tokens take a thousand keys, not half a million.
size/shape: Look inside one block's cache after seven tokens. The keys are seven rows, one per token, each a vector of d numbers: a seven by d array. The values make another.
size/grow: Write one more token, and each gains a row: eight by d. The width stays d.
size/stack: Every block keeps a cache of its own. Stack four blocks' key caches, block first, and they make one array: four, by seven, by d. The values make another.
size/memory: The price is memory. Say d is six. Then one block's keys hold seven rows of six: forty-two numbers.
size/pair: Its values hold forty-two more, so one block keeps eighty-four.
size/total: Four blocks keep four times that: three hundred thirty-six numbers.
size/general: In general, two, for keys and values, times the blocks, times the tokens, times d. And every sequence being written keeps a cache of its own.
